extracted.intended_audience: writers and other creative professionals (aspiring and professional) seeking self-care and sustainable writing practices
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and practical standards for maintaining mental wellness (self-care) while engaging in writing as a career or serious hobby, including productivity, accommodations, and therapeutic uses of writing. Focus is on sustainable habits, coping with bad times, and practical exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental wellness = self-care (not mental illness)
rubrics_metrics.description: For the purposes of this discussion, 'mental wellness' is not about coping with mental illness; it’s about self-care — practices to stay creative, productive, healthy, and happy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish this topic from clinical mental-health interventions; this rubric focuses on self-care actions and process-management for writing rather than diagnosis or treatment. The hosts note prior episodes address writing with depression, but this episode centers on everyday wellness practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical and mental wellness go together
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical wellness and mental wellness are interconnected; taking care of the body supports mental clarity and creative capacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include daily yoga or stretching, walking, showers, facemasks — any short activity that removes productivity metrics and provides a pass/fail self-care moment. Use physical activity to mitigate chronic pain or anxiety when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat writing as work and avoid burnout
rubrics_metrics.description: Remember writing is work even when enjoyable; intense, prolonged work without limits leads to emptiness and burnout.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anecdote: extreme schedules (e.g., working 6 AM to midnight daily) can be survivable short-term but cause long-term harm. Plan for limits and recovery rather than assuming endless stamina.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set boundaries and carve out non-work time
rubrics_metrics.description: When you set your own hours, deliberately create boundaries (scheduled off-work blocks) to protect family/time and prevent constant on-call creativity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: pick specific times that are always non-work (Brandon’s 5:30–9:30). Train yourself to 'turn the clock off' so you can recharge. Structure reduces guilt about unplugging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create sustainable practices for a long career
rubrics_metrics.description: Favor habits and routines that are maintainable over years rather than intense bursts you cannot sustain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short-term heroics are possible but not desirable for a long-standing career; design routines that permit continued productivity without repeated burnouts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not equate word count or output with self-worth
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid measuring your self-worth by daily word counts or quantity of output.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When under stress or in valleys, reduce expectations: the goal can be opening the document, thinking about the story, or producing a paragraph rather than a chapter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the smallest possible goals (micro-goals / 20-minute sprints)
rubrics_metrics.description: Carve tasks down to the smallest actionable unit (e.g., 20-minute sprints) so even bad days allow meaningful creative activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Victoria’s method: 20-minute sprints repeated across the day (e.g., nine sprints = three hours). Neil Gaiman’s heuristic: when sitting to write, your options are either write or do nothing; remove distractions to make the small choice easier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crack the seal — start small to overcome inertia
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin with a tiny action to break through overwhelming feelings; getting anything down helps momentum and reduces anxiety about a task.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even a few sentences or a short period of focused thought helps prop the creative door open and makes subsequent work easier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt routine and use accommodations for physical ailments
rubrics_metrics.description: When dealing with chronic or acute physical problems, be willing to change work setup and routines (standing desks, alternative keyboards, varied locations) to continue writing comfortably.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test different accommodations; what sticks becomes part of sustainable practice. Examples: standing desk, split keyboards, different typing posture/layouts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Listen to healthcare professionals and heed limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Some coping strategies (e.g., excessive ibuprofen) can be harmful; consult and follow medical advice to avoid long-term damage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be willing to step back from 'superhero' solutions and accept medical guidance; ignoring warning signs is an anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use accountability partners to avoid overdoing
rubrics_metrics.description: Have someone (friend, partner) who can check in and warn you when you’re burning out or neglecting basics like eating and rest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If available, a simple check-in can prevent unhealthy fixation; recognize that not everyone has this support, but cultivate it where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use writing as therapy thoughtfully and privately
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing can be cathartic — to process anger or grief — but when writing for personal therapy, the purpose is to have written rather than to publish or be read.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Techniques: write disconnected from the internet, print and delete files, tear up the paper and let it go. These preserve catharsis without unintended public consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outline to place emotional beats and write them when ready
rubrics_metrics.description: Use outlining to map emotional beats so you can write them out of order when your mental state matches the beat’s requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Block emotional scenes in advance so you can choose to write the ones you’re prepared for on a given day; this reduces pressure to be ready for every scene sequentially.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept creative fallow periods; broaden definition of 'writing'
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that 'writing' includes thinking, deleting, walking, musing, reading — and that fallow periods where output is low can be productive preparation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When you can’t produce, consume: read, watch, replenish the creative well. Don’t treat absence of output as failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use pen-and-paper to reduce digital distractions
rubrics_metrics.description: Switch to pen and paper to turn off extra digital voices and restart creative thinking when screens feel official or intimidating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scribbling, doodling, or making notes by hand breaks the blank-page anxiety; what you write on paper may not be final but it reopens the door.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build a lifestyle tracker to create daily small wins
rubrics_metrics.description: Create a grid tracking craft-oriented tasks (reading, writing, plotting) and non-craft self-care tasks (exercise, healthy eating, stretching) across days; color squares when done.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track for a 10–30 day period; goal is daily fresh starts so a missed hour doesn’t become a missed week. Use short trackers (e.g., 10 days) if 30 is overwhelming. Emphasize small wins (30 minutes of self-care counts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Discuss strategies with peers to find personalized solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Workshopping personal bad-times strategies with a group helps surface diverse techniques and unlock new approaches that might fit you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Host or join 'unlocking' sessions where multiple writers share tactics, because individual strategies vary widely and peer brainstorming can generate practical fixes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor responses to the specific kind of 'bad time'
rubrics_metrics.description: Bad times are heterogeneous; sometimes the best response is to stop writing, other times to change schedule, diet, or exercise to carve out writing time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no single answer—evaluate whether the issue calls for rest, logistical changes, or targeted self-care and respond accordingly.
